note: Curriculum-review artifact, not finished lesson prose. Sequenced pedagogically, not alphabetically. Every learning point traces to at least one evidence-requirement claim in EVIDENCE-RESULTS.json. This inventory is proposed only -- no learning point here is Product-Architect-approved, and none has been used to generate a lesson, storyboard, or assessment.
paCorrectionNote: Product Architect narrow correction pass (this session): HOLD -- NARROW CORRECTION verdict on the original 20-learning-point inventory. This is a one-time, pre-freeze renumbering, explicitly authorized by the Product Architect, not a reopening of the acquisition. Two structural changes were made, netting to the same total of 20: (1) the original combined resistivity/R=rho*L/A learning point is split into two independently-diagnosable outcomes -- resistivity's meaning/symbol/unit (now EFS-LP-06) and using the formula R=rho*L/A (now EFS-LP-07) -- because a learner can know what resistivity IS without yet being able to apply the formula, or vice versa; (2) the standalone fuse-operation learning point is removed, and its evidence requirement (fuse-operation-as-an-example-of-the-thermal-effect) is remapped to the thermal-effect learning point (now EFS-LP-19), since fuse operation is taught as a practical application/example of the same thermal effect, not as its own independently-assessed mastery outcome. All learning points from EFS-LP-08 onward are renumbered one position later than in the original inventory to accommodate the resistivity split, then the removal of the standalone fuse point brings the final count back to exactly 20 (see the identityFreezePolicy note below on why this renumbering is permitted only because the inventory is still proposed, not frozen). Six wording/technical corrections were also applied -- see the affected learning points' own depthJustification/knowledgeOrProcedure fields, and EVIDENCE-RESULTS.json's own paCorrectionNote for the underlying evidence-level rationale.
crossDomainPrerequisiteNote: Cross-domain prerequisites reference the accepted, frozen Batch 01 foundational-mathematics inventory (FM-LP-01 through FM-LP-25, reports/unit202-production-acquisition/batch-01-foundational-mathematics/FOUNDATIONAL-MATHEMATICS-LEARNING-POINTS.json). No FM-LP-* ID is edited, renumbered, or duplicated here; only genuine prerequisites are recorded, not every mathematically-adjacent ID. Product Architect correction (this pass): FM-LP-04 (the four operations on decimals) is now attached to every learning point with an explicit numerical calculation outcome (EFS-LP-02, 07, 08, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18); FM-LP-13 (substitution/order of operations) is removed from EFS-LP-05 (resistance), which is now purely definitional and carries no calculation outcome of its own -- arithmetic prerequisites are not attached to purely conceptual/definitional learning points.

learningPoints.title: Basic electron theory
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to describe the basic structure of an atom (nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounding electrons) and explain that a material conducts electricity when its outer electrons are free to move.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: An atom has a tiny nucleus (protons and neutrons) surrounded by electrons equal in number to the protons, making it electrically neutral. In some materials, outer electrons are loosely bound and free to move through the material; this electron mobility is the physical basis of electrical conduction.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Matches Unit 202's Level 2 depth: atomic structure and electron mobility as the qualitative basis for conduction, not quantum/band theory.
explicitExclusions: Electron shells/orbitals and quantum energy levels
Band theory of conduction
Ionisation and ion formation
applicationTypes: Explain, in outline, why a copper wire conducts electricity but a plastic sheath does not.

learningPoints.title: Current as the rate of flow of electric charge
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge and use the relationship between current, charge and time.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge past a point in a circuit (I = charge/time); the ampere, its SI unit, is one coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
learningPoints.depthJustification: Calibrated deliberately to teach current AS charge flow (the correct definition) with electron motion as the physical carrier in a conductor, not as an equivalent restatement -- this is the exact false-green risk the acquisition brief for this batch flagged, and this outcome is worded to avoid it. Product Architect correction (this pass): FM-LP-04 (decimal arithmetic) added, since this learning point has an explicit numerical calculation outcome (charge = current x time).
explicitExclusions: Drift velocity calculations
Charge-carrier density/microscopic conduction theory
applicationTypes: Calculate the charge that has flowed in a given time for a stated steady current.

learningPoints.title: Conventional current and electron flow
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that conventional current is defined as the direction in which positive charge would move, describe how this applies to the external circuit of a DC source, and distinguish it from the actual electron-drift direction in a metallic conductor.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Conventional current is defined as the direction in which positive charge would move. In the external metallic circuit of a DC source, this is commonly described as flowing from the positive terminal towards the negative terminal -- but this is a description of that particular case, not an unqualified rule for every physical situation. In a metallic conductor the actual charge carriers are electrons, which physically drift in the opposite direction to conventional current. Both descriptions are self-consistent and give identical results for circuit calculations.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-ELECUR: conventional current vs electron flow
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept as its own learning point (not merged into EFS-LP-02) so a learner who understands current-as-charge-flow but still confuses the two directional conventions can be diagnosed separately -- a genuinely common, independent misconception at this level. Product Architect correction (this pass): the outcome and procedure no longer present 'positive to negative' as an unqualified universal rule -- conventional current is defined generally as the direction positive charge would move, with the positive-to-negative description scoped explicitly to the external circuit of a DC source.
explicitExclusions: Historical/Franklin biographical detail beyond the reason for the convention
Semiconductor hole-flow direction
applicationTypes: Label the conventional-current and electron-flow arrows on a simple battery-and-resistor circuit diagram.

learningPoints.title: Conductors and insulators
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain the difference between a conductor and an insulator in terms of resistivity and electron mobility, and give an example of each.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A conductor (e.g. copper) has loosely bound outer electrons free to move, so charge moves relatively readily through it because it has comparatively low resistance/resistivity. An insulator (e.g. glass) has tightly bound electrons, so it strongly opposes charge movement and carries only negligible or extremely small current at ordinary applied voltages, because it has very high resistivity.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Conductors and insulators are combined into one learning point because they are two poles of the same single comparison, always taught and assessed together at this level -- separating them would create an artificial fragment, not a genuinely independent diagnosis. Product Architect correction (this pass): an insulator is not defined as absolutely preventing current, nor a conductor as allowing current to flow with no opposition at all -- both are now stated with comparatively-qualified wording (relatively readily / comparatively low resistance; strongly opposes / negligible or extremely small current), without expanding into semiconductor theory, dielectric breakdown, or band theory.
explicitExclusions: Semiconductors
Superconductivity
Dielectric breakdown voltage
applicationTypes: Classify a list of everyday materials (copper, rubber, glass, aluminium, PVC) as conductors or insulators and justify each.

learningPoints.title: Resistance
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state the definition of electrical resistance and its unit.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Resistance is the ratio of the voltage applied across a component to the current that flows through it (R = V/I), measured in ohms (Ω).
learningPoints.depthJustification: Definitional depth only; calculation practice is covered once Ohm's law itself is taught (EFS-LP-08). Product Architect correction (this pass): the FM-LP-13 (substitution/order of operations) cross-domain prerequisite is removed -- this learning point remains a pure definition (what resistance is, and its unit) with no calculation outcome of its own, so it should not carry an arithmetic prerequisite.
explicitExclusions: Non-ohmic/variable-resistance devices
Temperature-coefficient-of-resistance calculations
applicationTypes: State the unit of electrical resistance and what its ratio compares.

learningPoints.title: Resistivity: meaning, symbol and unit
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain the distinction between resistance and resistivity, identify resistivity as a property of a material (not of a particular conductor's shape), and state its symbol (ρ) and its SI unit (ohm-metre, Ω·m).
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Resistivity (symbol ρ, unit ohm-metre, Ω·m) is a property of a material itself, independent of a particular conductor's shape or size -- unlike resistance, which also depends on the conductor's length and cross-sectional area.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-RESIS: resistivity as a material property
learningPoints.depthJustification: Product Architect correction (this pass): split from the original combined resistivity/R=rho*L/A learning point into two independently-diagnosable outcomes. This learning point covers resistivity's meaning, symbol and unit only -- a learner can know that resistivity is a shape-independent material property with symbol rho and unit ohm-metre without yet being able to use R=rho*L/A (now EFS-LP-07), and the reverse is equally possible (a learner might apply the formula mechanically without grasping what resistivity itself represents). Kept separate from EFS-LP-05 (resistance) because resistivity-as-a-shape-independent-material-constant is a genuinely distinct, commonly-confused idea from a component's V/I ratio.
explicitExclusions: Temperature dependence of resistivity
Resistivity of semiconductors/superconductors
The formula R=rho*L/A itself (see EFS-LP-07)
applicationTypes: Explain why two wires of the same length and cross-sectional area but different materials can have different resistances.
State the symbol and SI unit used for resistivity.

learningPoints.title: Using R = ρL/A
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to identify R, ρ, L and A in the formula R = ρL/A, explain qualitatively how resistance changes with resistivity, length and cross-sectional area, and calculate or rearrange the formula for an unknown quantity.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: R = ρL/A relates a conductor's resistance R (ohms) to its resistivity ρ (ohm-metres), its length L (metres) and its cross-sectional area A (square metres): resistance increases with length and resistivity, and decreases as cross-sectional area increases. The formula can be rearranged to find ρ, L or A when the other three quantities are known.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Product Architect correction (this pass): split from the original combined resistivity/R=rho*L/A learning point (see EFS-LP-06) so that using the formula -- identifying its terms, reasoning qualitatively about how R changes with rho/L/A, and calculating or rearranging for an unknown -- is a separately-diagnosable outcome from knowing what resistivity itself is. Rearranging R=rho*L/A is treated as an application of the general formula-transposition skill already evidenced for Unit 202's foundational-mathematics batch (FM-LP-16), consistent with EVIDENCE-RESULTS.json's own scopeNote for this requirement, which discloses that neither retrieved source shows the formula explicitly rearranged in text.
explicitExclusions: Anisotropic/non-uniform conductors
Deriving R=rho*L/A from first principles (the microscopic derivation is confirming evidence only, not a taught outcome)
applicationTypes: Given a cable's resistivity, length and cross-sectional area, calculate its resistance.
Explain why doubling a conductor's cross-sectional area halves its resistance.
Rearrange R=rho*L/A to find the length of a conductor given its resistance, resistivity and cross-sectional area.

learningPoints.title: Ohm's law: V = IR and rearrangements
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state Ohm's law as a conditional relationship for ohmic conductors and use V=IR and its rearrangements (I=V/R, R=V/I) to calculate an unknown voltage, current or resistance.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: For an ohmic conductor, current is directly proportional to the voltage applied across it (resistance is constant over a wide range of voltages); V = IR relates voltage V (volts), current I (amperes) and resistance R (ohms), and rearranges to I = V/R and R = V/I. Ohm's law is a property of ohmic materials, not a universal law true for every component.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-HP-OHMLAW: Ohm's law and V=IR rearrangements
learningPoints.depthJustification: The conceptual relationship (Ohm's law) and its formula/rearrangements are combined into one learning point because they are the same single relationship viewed from two angles -- a learner who 'knows Ohm's law' and one who 'can use V=IR and its rearrangements' are exhibiting the same skill, and splitting them would be an artificial fragment. Deliberately worded as a conditional (ohmic-material) relationship, not an unrestricted universal law, per the depth guidance for this batch.
explicitExclusions: Non-ohmic devices (diodes, thermistors, filament lamps at varying temperature)
AC impedance/reactance
applicationTypes: Calculate the current through a known resistor given the supply voltage.
Rearrange V=IR to find the resistance of a component from measured voltage and current.

learningPoints.title: Voltage drop across resistance
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain what a voltage drop is and state that the voltage drop across a resistance carrying current I is Vdrop = IR.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A voltage drop is the potential difference (loss of voltage) that appears across a resistance as a result of current flowing through it; the voltage drop across a resistance R carrying current I is Vdrop = IR -- the same relationship as Ohm's law, applied to describe the voltage lost across that specific resistance.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-UTAH-OHMSLAW: voltage drop across a resistor, V=IR
learningPoints.depthJustification: Definition and formula combined for the same reason as Ohm's law (EFS-LP-08): they are one concept, not two. Kept separate from EFS-LP-10 (the calculation procedure) because understanding what a voltage drop IS and being able to CALCULATE one in a real cable/circuit scenario are genuinely different, independently-diagnosable skills.
explicitExclusions: AC voltage drop with reactance/power factor
Voltage-drop compensation devices
applicationTypes: State the voltage drop across a 5 ohm resistor carrying 2 A.

learningPoints.title: Calculating voltage drop
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to calculate the voltage drop in a cable run given its tabulated voltage-drop factor, the design current and the cable length, and compare the result with the stated or applicable design criterion for the problem.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A cable's voltage drop is calculated as (tabulated mV/A/m factor) x (design current) x (circuit length) / 1000, giving the drop in volts. This calculated value is then compared with the stated or applicable design criterion for the problem -- for example, BS 7671 Table 4Ab's recommended (informative) value of 5% for a load other than lighting supplied directly from a public low-voltage distribution system -- not assumed against a single universal permitted figure, since the acceptable voltage drop in a real design depends on the requirements of the connected equipment.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-IET-VDROP: voltage-drop calculation procedure and Table 4Ab's context-specific recommended value
learningPoints.depthJustification: Scoped to the calculation procedure only, at a depth appropriate for Unit 202 foundational depth; does not extend into full cable-selection compliance (correction factors, overcurrent-device coordination), which belongs to a later, more advanced stage of electrical installation study. Product Architect correction (this pass): the outcome and procedure no longer instruct the learner to check a calculated voltage drop against a universal 'permitted maximum' -- the source establishes a recommended, informative value for one specific context (non-lighting loads from a public LV distribution system), and the corrected wording directs the learner to compare against the stated or applicable design criterion for the problem at hand. No separate mastery point is created for the 5% example; it remains one illustration within this same learning point.
explicitExclusions: Correction factors (Ca, Cg, Ci, Cc) for cable current rating
Three-phase voltage-drop calculations
Reactive (AC) voltage-drop components
Treating 5% as a universal permitted maximum applicable to every design
applicationTypes: Calculate the voltage drop for a given cable's mV/A/m rating, a stated load current, and a stated cable run length, and compare it with a stated design criterion (which may or may not be 5%, depending on the equipment and supply arrangement described).

learningPoints.title: Series circuit: current
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that the current is the same at every point in a series circuit.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a series circuit, the same current flows through every component, because there is only one path for charge to follow: I = I1 = I2 = ...
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept as its own learning point (mirroring the frozen plan's own separation of series current/resistance/voltage into three distinct requirements) because current, resistance and voltage behaviour in a series circuit are three separately-diagnosable relationships -- a learner may master one while still misapplying another, which is exactly the false-green risk this batch's brief names for series/parallel relationships.
explicitExclusions: Multi-loop/non-series-only networks (Kirchhoff's rules)
AC series circuits with reactance
applicationTypes: State the current through the second of three lamps wired in series, given the current through the first.

learningPoints.title: Series circuit: total resistance
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to calculate the total (equivalent) resistance of resistors connected in series.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The equivalent resistance of resistors connected in series is the sum of their individual resistances: Req = R1 + R2 + ... + RN.
learningPoints.depthJustification: See EFS-LP-11 for the rationale for keeping series current/resistance/voltage as separate learning points. Product Architect correction (this pass): FM-LP-04 (decimal arithmetic) added as a genuine numerical-calculation prerequisite.
explicitExclusions: Series-parallel network reduction (covered once both series and parallel rules are taught)
applicationTypes: Calculate the total resistance of three named resistors connected in series.

learningPoints.title: Series circuit: voltage sharing
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that the supply voltage in a series circuit is shared among the resistors in proportion to their resistance, and that the individual voltage drops sum to the supply voltage.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a series circuit, the supply voltage is divided among the resistors in proportion to their resistance, and the sum of the individual voltage drops equals the total supply voltage: deltaV = deltaV1 + deltaV2 + ..., where each deltaVi = I*Ri (the same current I flows through each).
learningPoints.depthJustification: See EFS-LP-11 for the rationale for keeping series current/resistance/voltage as separate learning points; voltage sharing is proportional reasoning applied to resistance ratios, hence the FM-LP-10 (direct proportion) cross-domain prerequisite. Product Architect correction (this pass): FM-LP-04 (decimal arithmetic) added alongside FM-LP-10.
explicitExclusions: Voltage-divider circuits with a loaded output (a separate, more advanced application)
applicationTypes: Given three series resistors and a supply voltage, calculate the voltage drop across each.

learningPoints.title: Parallel circuit: voltage
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that the voltage is the same across every branch of a parallel circuit.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a parallel circuit, the voltage (potential difference) across every branch is the same and equal to the supply voltage: deltaV = deltaV1 = deltaV2 = ...
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from parallel current/resistance for the same reason series current/resistance/voltage are kept separate (see EFS-LP-11) -- each is independently diagnosable and a frequent, distinct source of learner confusion.
explicitExclusions: Non-ideal (loaded) sources with internal resistance affecting branch voltages
applicationTypes: State the voltage across the second of three lamps wired in parallel, given the supply voltage.

learningPoints.title: Parallel circuit: current
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that current divides among the branches of a parallel circuit and that the branch currents sum to the total current.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: In a parallel circuit, the total current divides among the branches, and the individual branch currents sum to the total current entering (and leaving) the parallel combination: I = I1 + I2 + ...
learningPoints.depthJustification: See EFS-LP-14/EFS-LP-11. Product Architect correction (this pass): FM-LP-04 (decimal arithmetic) added as a genuine numerical-calculation prerequisite (e.g. finding a branch current from the total and other branches).
explicitExclusions: Kirchhoff's current law for general (non-simple-parallel) networks
applicationTypes: Given the current through two of three parallel branches and the total supply current, find the current through the third branch.

learningPoints.title: Parallel circuit: equivalent resistance
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to calculate the equivalent resistance of resistors connected in parallel.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The equivalent (total) resistance of resistors in parallel is found from 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... + 1/RN.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Combining reciprocal resistances requires fraction arithmetic (adding fractions with unlike denominators, then taking a reciprocal) -- exactly the skill Batch 01's own inventory flagged as a foundational prerequisite for 'parallel-resistance-style formulae' (see FOUNDATIONAL-MATHEMATICS-LEARNING-POINTS.json's foundationalPrerequisitesForElectricalCalculations list), so FM-LP-01/FM-LP-02 are recorded here as the genuine cross-domain prerequisite that batch anticipated. Product Architect correction (this pass): the outcome and knowledge/procedure no longer assert that the equivalent resistance is always smaller than the smallest individual branch resistance -- that assertion was this session's own prior inference, not a statement drawn from either retrieved source, and is not required by this requirement's evidence plan; it has been removed. FM-LP-04 (decimal arithmetic) added alongside FM-LP-01/FM-LP-02.
explicitExclusions: The product-over-sum shortcut for exactly two resistors (a calculation convenience, not separately assessed knowledge)
applicationTypes: Calculate the equivalent resistance of two or three named resistors connected in parallel.

learningPoints.title: Electrical power formulas
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state the three equivalent forms of the electrical power formula and select the appropriate one for the quantities known in a given calculation.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: Electrical power is the product of voltage and current, P = VI. Using Ohm's law (V=IR), this is equivalent to P = I^2R (used when current and resistance are known) and to P = V^2/R (used when voltage and resistance are known). For P=V^2/R, V and R must refer to the same component or equivalent load -- if a source's emf is substituted for the actual voltage across the load (rather than the load's own terminal voltage), that substitution is only valid where the source's own internal resistance is negligible compared with the load; the formula P=V^2/R itself has no such requirement when V is the actual voltage across the resistance in question.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-ETSU-PHYS2020: P=(deltaV)^2/Req, with the emf-substitution condition correctly isolated
learningPoints.depthJustification: The three power forms are combined into one learning point because they are algebraically equivalent expressions of a single relationship, and the frozen requirement plan itself frames 'the conditions under which P=VI, P=I^2R and P=V^2/R are used' as one combined concern -- unlike series/parallel relationships, these are not separately-taught facts but one relationship viewed three ways. Product Architect correction (this pass): the condition attached to P=V^2/R no longer implies the formula itself requires negligible source/internal resistance. The corrected wording states that P=V^2/R applies whenever V is the actual voltage across the resistance in question, and that negligible internal resistance is relevant only to the separate step of substituting a source's emf for the load's actual terminal voltage -- learners must choose V, I and R values that refer to the same component or equivalent load.
explicitExclusions: AC power with power factor/reactive power
Energy (kWh) calculations from power and time (a distinct, not-yet-acquired Unit 202 topic)
applicationTypes: Given a resistor's current and resistance, calculate the power dissipated using the most appropriate formula.
Explain which power formula to use when only voltage and resistance are known.

learningPoints.title: Calculating power in a DC circuit
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to carry out a DC-circuit power calculation: reduce a network of series and parallel resistors to a single equivalent resistance, then apply the appropriate power formula.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: A suitable procedure for a DC-circuit power calculation is: (1) reduce the circuit's series and parallel resistor combinations step by step to a single equivalent resistance; (2) apply the appropriate power relationship (P=VI, P=I^2R or P=V^2/R, as the known quantities allow, and ensuring V, I and R all refer to the same component or equivalent load) to find the required unknown.
normalizedClaimRefs: SRC-ETSU-PHYS2020: worked multi-resistor DC power-calculation example
learningPoints.depthJustification: Kept separate from EFS-LP-17 (the power-formula concept) because carrying out a full multi-step DC circuit calculation (network reduction, then formula selection and application) is a distinct, more demanding procedural skill from knowing the formulas themselves -- a learner may know all three formulas but not yet be able to apply them within a multi-resistor network. Product Architect correction (this pass): FM-LP-04 (decimal arithmetic) added alongside FM-LP-16.
explicitExclusions: Multi-loop networks requiring Kirchhoff's rules (not reducible to simple series/parallel combination)
applicationTypes: Given a network of series and parallel resistors and a supply voltage, calculate the total power delivered by the source.

learningPoints.title: Thermal effect of electric current
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to state that current flowing through a resistance generates heat, that the rate of heat generation is proportional to the square of the current for a fixed resistance and time, and explain how a fuse uses this effect to protect a circuit from excessive current.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The thermal effect of current (Joule heating) is the conversion of electrical energy into heat as current flows through a resistance; the rate of heat production is P=I^2R=IV, so for a fixed resistance and time, it increases with the square of the current. A fuse is a practical application of this effect: it contains a thin conductor that melts at a designed (low) temperature, and when the circuit current becomes high enough to generate sufficient heat to reach that melting point, the conductor melts and interrupts the circuit.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Product Architect correction (this pass): the original standalone fuse-operation learning point is removed, and its evidence requirement is remapped here. Fuse operation is taught as a practical application/example of the thermal effect -- excessive current produces heating in the fuse element, which melts and interrupts the circuit -- not as its own independently-assessed mastery outcome; independent mastery of fuse construction, fuse types, selection, coordination, regulations, or fault-protection design is explicitly out of scope for this batch. The current-squared heating relationship is also now qualified as holding for a fixed resistance and time, since power is itself a rate and resistance is not assumed constant in general.
explicitExclusions: Specific heat capacity/temperature-rise calculations
Heat dissipation/cooling engineering
Fuse rating selection/coordination with cable current-carrying capacity
Circuit-breaker/MCB operating mechanisms (a different protective device)
Fuse types, construction, or fault-protection design as independently-assessed knowledge
applicationTypes: Explain why doubling the current through a fixed resistor quadruples the rate of heat generated.
Explain, in terms of the thermal effect, why a fuse rated for a lower current than the fault current will break the circuit.

learningPoints.title: Chemical effect and electrolysis
learningPoints.learnerOutcome: The learner will be able to explain, in outline, how passing an electric current through an electrolyte causes a chemical reaction, and describe what happens at the anode and cathode.
learningPoints.knowledgeOrProcedure: The chemical effect of an electric current (electrolysis) is the chemical decomposition of a substance caused by passing a current through it via an electrolyte: oxidation occurs at the positive electrode (anode) and reduction occurs at the negative electrode (cathode), producing new substances -- for example, passing current through water containing an electrolyte decomposes it into hydrogen gas at the cathode and oxygen gas at the anode.
learningPoints.depthJustification: Matches Level 2 depth: qualitative mechanism (electrolyte, anode/cathode roles, oxidation/reduction, decomposition) via a single worked example, not electrochemical cell potentials or Faraday's laws of electrolysis. Unchanged in this correction pass other than renumbering.
explicitExclusions: Faraday's laws of electrolysis (quantitative mass/charge relationships)
Electrode potentials and the electrochemical series
Industrial electrolysis processes (e.g. aluminium extraction) beyond a passing example
Ionic equations beyond the single worked example
applicationTypes: State which gas is produced at the cathode when water containing a suitable electrolyte is electrolysed.

identityFreezePolicy.status: NOT FROZEN -- proposed for Product Architect review; one pre-freeze renumbering authorized and applied in this pass
identityFreezePolicy.note: Unlike the accepted Batch 01 FM-LP-* inventory, these EFS-LP-* IDs are not yet an approved identity baseline. The Product Architect explicitly authorized one renumbering of this still-proposed inventory in this correction pass (splitting the resistivity/R=rho*L/A learning point and removing the standalone fuse learning point). No renumbering of this kind is permitted once this inventory is accepted and frozen -- from that point on, the same discipline FM-LP-* is already held to would apply: an ID is never reassigned, future genuinely-new learning points would be appended (EFS-LP-21 onward) rather than inserted, and instructional order is tracked separately from identity via the instructionalSequence field below.
